days.title: Tools of Genetic Engineering
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Identify the tools used in genetic engineering.
  • Describe restriction enzymes.
  • Explain the role of plasmids and vectors.
  • Describe DNA ligase and gel electrophoresis.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Restriction enzyme — cuts DNA at specific sequences.
  • Plasmid — circular DNA vector.
  • DNA ligase — seals DNA fragments.
  • Gel electrophoresis — separates DNA by size.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Tools of Genetic Engineering

ToolFunction
Restriction enzymeCuts DNA at specific sites
DNA ligaseSeals DNA fragments together
PlasmidCarrier/vector for DNA
Gel electrophoresisSeparates fragments by size
PCRAmplifies DNA

B. Why Restriction Enzymes?

They produce sticky ends that allow complementary base pairing — essential for building recombinant DNA.

💬 Let's Discuss

Genetic engineering is the direct, deliberate change of an organism's DNA, often by moving a gene from one organism into another. It depends on a small toolkit, much of it borrowed from bacteria.

Restriction enzymes are "molecular scissors." Bacteria use them to chop up the DNA of invading viruses. Each enzyme cuts at a specific short sequence; for example, EcoRI cuts at GAATTC. Many cut in a staggered way, leaving short single-stranded overhangs called sticky ends. Any two pieces of DNA cut with the same enzyme have matching sticky ends that can base-pair — whether they came from a human or a bacterium. DNA ligase is the "molecular glue" that seals the backbone, joining the pieces permanently.

A vector carries the gene into a host cell. The most common vector is a plasmid, a small circle of bacterial DNA that copies itself independently and often carries an antibiotic-resistance gene useful for selection. Viruses can also serve as vectors.

Two techniques let scientists handle tiny amounts of DNA. PCR (polymerase chain reaction) copies a chosen DNA segment millions of times in a few hours by repeated heating and cooling with a heat-stable DNA polymerase; it is used in COVID-19 tests and forensic work. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size: DNA is negatively charged, so it moves toward the positive electrode through a gel, and smaller pieces travel farther. The band pattern is used in DNA fingerprinting and paternity testing.

Common mistake: thinking PCR separates DNA or that electrophoresis copies it. PCR amplifies; electrophoresis sorts by size.

pairs.why: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific recognition sequences.
DNA ligase seals the sugar–phosphate backbone between fragments.
A plasmid is a circular DNA used to carry genes into bacteria.
Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size.
PCR makes millions of copies of a DNA segment.
Staggered cuts leave single-stranded overhangs — sticky ends.

questions.explanation: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences.

days.title: Steps in Creating Recombinant DNA
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Outline the steps in creating recombinant DNA.
  • Explain gene cloning.
  • Describe transformation of bacteria.
  • Explain selection of successful recombinants.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Recombinant DNA — DNA combining sequences from different sources.
  • Transformation — uptake of foreign DNA by bacteria.
  • Selection — identifying bacteria that took up the plasmid.
  • Gene cloning — producing many copies of a gene.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Steps in Creating Recombinant DNA

  1. Isolate gene of interest
  2. Cut plasmid with same restriction enzyme
  3. Ligate gene into plasmid
  4. Introduce plasmid into bacteria (transformation)
  5. Select successful recombinants
  6. Grow bacteria — they produce the gene product

B. Example: Human Insulin

The human insulin gene is inserted into E. coli plasmids. Bacteria produce insulin, which is harvested and purified.

💬 Let's Discuss

Recombinant DNA is DNA that combines sequences from two different sources. The classic example — and one of the first great successes of biotechnology — is making human insulin in bacteria. Before 1982, people with diabetes used insulin extracted from cow and pig pancreases, which was limited and sometimes caused allergies.

The process follows six steps. 1. Isolate the gene: the human insulin gene is obtained and cut out with a restriction enzyme. 2. Cut the plasmid: a plasmid is opened with the same restriction enzyme, so both have matching sticky ends. 3. Ligate: the gene and plasmid are mixed; sticky ends pair, and DNA ligase seals them, forming a recombinant plasmid. 4. Transform: bacteria such as E. coli are treated (with calcium salts and a heat shock) so that some take up the plasmid. 5. Select: bacteria are grown on a medium with an antibiotic. Only bacteria carrying the plasmid's antibiotic-resistance gene survive; further tests identify those carrying the insulin gene. 6. Produce: the selected bacteria are grown in huge fermentation tanks. Every time they divide, they copy the plasmid — this is gene cloning — and they make human insulin, which is purified for patients.

The same method produces human growth hormone, clotting factors for hemophilia and the hepatitis B vaccine (in yeast). It works because the genetic code is universal: bacteria read human codons the same way human cells do.

Common mistake: using two different restriction enzymes for the gene and plasmid. The ends would not match; the same enzyme must cut both.

pairs.why: Recombinant DNA combines DNA from different sources.
Transformation is the uptake of foreign DNA by bacteria.
Selection identifies bacteria that took up the recombinant plasmid.
Gene cloning makes many copies of a gene as bacteria multiply.
Engineered E. coli produce human insulin for diabetics.

days.title: Applications of Recombinant DNA
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Identify real-world applications of recombinant DNA.
  • Describe medical applications.
  • Describe agricultural applications.
  • Explain industrial uses.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Medicine — insulin, vaccines, gene therapy.
  • Agriculture — pest-resistant crops, Golden Rice.
  • Industry — enzymes, biofuels.
  • Research — gene function studies.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Medical Applications

  • Human insulin for diabetes
  • Human growth hormone
  • Hepatitis B vaccine
  • Gene therapy

B. Agricultural Applications

  • Bt corn (pest-resistant)
  • Golden Rice (Vitamin A)
  • Herbicide-resistant soybeans
  • Drought-tolerant crops

C. Industrial Applications

  • Enzymes for detergents and food
  • Biofuels from engineered microbes
  • Bioremediation of pollutants

💬 Let's Discuss

Recombinant DNA technology has moved from the laboratory into hospitals, farms and factories. It helps to sort applications into three groups.

Medical. Bacteria make human insulin for diabetics and growth hormone for children with growth problems. Yeast makes the hepatitis B vaccine by producing just a harmless virus surface protein. Some COVID-19 vaccines were made using recombinant viral vectors. Gene therapy delivers a working gene into a patient's cells to treat inherited disorders, and has treated some forms of inherited blindness and immune deficiency.

Agricultural. Bt corn and Bt eggplant carry a gene from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis that makes a protein toxic to certain insect larvae but harmless to people, so farmers spray less pesticide. Bt corn has been grown in the Philippines since 2003. Golden Rice, developed with the Philippine Rice Research Institute (PhilRice) and IRRI, makes beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, to help fight vitamin A deficiency that causes blindness in children. Other crops are engineered for drought tolerance or virus resistance (like papaya ringspot-resistant papaya).

Industrial and environmental. Engineered microbes produce enzymes for detergents and food processing, biofuels such as ethanol, and biodegradable plastics. In bioremediation, microbes break down pollutants such as oil spills and toxic chemicals.

Common mistake: thinking Bt crops contain "pesticide sprayed into them." The plant makes its own Bt protein from an inserted gene.

pairs.why: Engineered bacteria produce human insulin to treat diabetes.
Recombinant yeast make a hepatitis B surface protein for vaccines.
Bt corn makes its own insect-killing protein.
Golden Rice produces beta-carotene, a source of vitamin A.
Engineered microbes can produce fuels such as ethanol.
Bioremediation uses microbes to break down pollutants.

scenarios.explanation: Insulin from bacteria treats a disease — medical.

scenarios.explanation: A crop producing its own pesticide is agricultural.

scenarios.explanation: Beta-carotene rice is an agricultural application.

scenarios.explanation: Microbes cleaning oil spills is bioremediation.

scenarios.explanation: Vaccines made in yeast are medical.

scenarios.explanation: Gene therapy to treat a disorder is medical.

questions.explanation: The hepatitis B vaccine is a medical application.

takeaways: Recombinant DNA benefits medicine, agriculture, and industry.

days.title: Ethical Issues & Future Directions
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Identify ethical issues in genetic engineering.
  • Discuss pros and cons of GMOs.
  • Describe future directions in biotechnology.
  • Analyze bioethical dilemmas.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Bioethics — ethics of biological research.
  • GMO — genetically modified organism.
  • CRISPR — gene editing tool.
  • Gene therapy — correcting genetic disorders.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Ethical Concerns

  • Safety of GMO foods
  • Environmental impact (gene flow)
  • Designer babies
  • Privacy of genetic information
  • Access and cost of gene therapies

B. Future Directions

  • CRISPR-based therapies
  • Personalized medicine
  • Engineered organs
  • Synthetic biology

C. Balanced View

Recombinant DNA technology has transformed medicine, agriculture, and industry. Responsible use requires oversight, transparency, and ethical review.

💬 Let's Discuss

Because genetic engineering can change living things directly, it raises questions that science alone cannot answer. Bioethics is the study of what is right and wrong in biology and medicine.

Environmental concerns: genes from GMO crops could spread to wild relatives through pollen (gene flow), and pests may evolve resistance to Bt proteins. Safety and regulation: people ask whether GM foods are safe to eat. Major scientific bodies have found approved GM foods as safe as conventional ones, and in the Philippines they must pass evaluation under the Department of Agriculture's Bureau of Plant Industry before release. Still, the 2015 Supreme Court case on Bt eggplant field trials shows how much public debate exists.

Genetic privacy: if insurance companies or employers learned your genetic risks, they could discriminate against you. Who should own and see your DNA data? Access and equity: gene therapies can cost millions of pesos, so they may help only the wealthy. Designer babies: new tools such as CRISPR-Cas9 can edit genes precisely and cheaply. Editing body cells to cure disease is widely accepted; editing embryos so the changes are inherited — or choosing traits like height or eye color — is highly controversial. In 2018, a scientist in China was imprisoned for editing human embryos.

Future directions: personalized medicine (drugs chosen by your genes), faster vaccine design, CRISPR cures for sickle-cell disease, and climate-resilient crops.

When you evaluate an issue, weigh the benefits, risks, who is affected, and who decides. Common mistake: treating every GMO as either all good or all bad; each case should be judged on evidence.

pairs.why: Bioethics studies the moral questions raised by biology and medicine.
A GMO has DNA altered by genetic engineering.
CRISPR-Cas9 is a precise gene-editing tool.
Gene therapy adds or fixes genes to treat genetic disorders.
Genetic privacy is about who can see and use your DNA information.
Choosing a baby's traits by editing embryos is a major ethical dilemma.
